title: Willy Brandt Kneels in Warsaw
text:
On December 7, 1970, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was in Warsaw to sign a treaty with Poland accepting the postwar border and opening a new relationship between the two countries. Poland had suffered terribly under German occupation in the Second World War, and some six million Polish citizens, half of them Jews, had been killed.

That morning Brandt went to the monument to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943. He laid a wreath, straightened its ribbons and stepped back. Then, to the surprise of everyone around him, he dropped to his knees on the wet stone and stayed there in silence for about half a minute before rising.

Brandt himself had opposed the Nazis and spent the war in exile. The gesture was not in the program. He later wrote that, under the weight of recent German history, he had done what people do when words fail them.

At home the act was controversial; in a magazine poll many West Germans said it was excessive. But the photograph traveled around the world and became a lasting symbol of German acceptance of responsibility for the past. In 1971 Brandt received the Nobel Peace Prize for his policy of reconciliation with the East.
lesson: A sincere, humble gesture of apology can say what speeches cannot. When words would sound empty, let your actions show that you understand the harm done.
source: Contemporary press reports and photographs; Willy Brandt, People and Politics: The Years 1960-1975 (1976)
